\chapter{Five Everyday Actions}
\label{ch:entrar-y-volver}
\hlchaptermodality{395}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say entrar, volver, llegar, perder and necesitar, and name five everyday actions.}

Complete ES-C395-necesitar: name five everyday actions, and say one thing about each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[entrar]{entrar — the vowel that tells you how the word travelled}

\label{lesson:ES-C395-entrar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the guitar}, then \emph{the doctor}. (\emph{La guitarra}; \emph{el médico}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la puerta — what you go through.
  \item la entrada — the noun standing beside this verb.
  \item salir — the other direction.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{en-TRAR}, two beats with the weight on the second. Both \emph{r}'s are one quick tap of the tongue, not the long English \emph{r}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{entrar} — \textquotedblleft{}to go in.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{intrāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to go into,\textquotedblright{} built on \textbf{intrā}, \textquotedblleft{}within.\textquotedblright{}

The mark worth keeping is the first vowel. Latin's short \textbf{i} came down to Spanish as \textbf{e}, so \emph{intrāre} surfaced as \textbf{entrar}. That happened to words carried in the mouth, generation to generation, with nobody consulting a page.

Set it against a word that \emph{was} consulted from a page. The prefix \textbf{intra-} turns up in Spanish with its Latin \emph{i} intact — \emph{intravenoso}, \emph{intramuros} — because it was lifted out of written Latin long afterwards and had no journey to change it. Same Latin \emph{intrā}, two different routes, two different vowels.

English took the verb the long way round too, through Old French, and got \textbf{enter} — with the same lowered vowel. Beside it sit \textbf{entrance}, and the bookish \textbf{interior}, which kept its \emph{i} for the same reason \emph{intravenoso} did.

One thing English will not hand over: the grammar. English says \emph{enter the room} with nothing in between. Spanish puts a small word there.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{entrar \textbf{en} la habitación} — across Spain;
  \item \emph{entrar \textbf{a} la habitación} — across much of Latin America.
\end{itemize}

Neither is the careless one. The verb points at a direction; the little word attaches the place.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{entrar}. And you can read an initial \emph{entr-} as the fingerprint of a word that came through speech.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{entrar}
  \item \emph{entrar en la casa}
  \item \emph{la puerta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What became of the short \emph{i} of Latin \emph{intrāre}? (It dropped to \emph{e}.) So why does \emph{intravenoso} still show an \emph{i}? (It came out of written Latin long after the change had finished.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[volver]{volver — the o that breaks in two}

\label{lesson:ES-C395-volver}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the doctor}, then \emph{to go in}. (\emph{El médico}; \emph{entrar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la vuelta — the noun that came out of this verb.
  \item la puerta — the same \emph{o}, the same break.
  \item volar — the near neighbour that is not a relative.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bol-BER}, two beats with the weight on the second. Both \emph{v}'s are the soft Spanish \emph{b}; the \emph{ue} of \emph{vuelvo} is a quick \emph{weh}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{volver} — \textquotedblleft{}to return.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{volvere} meant \textquotedblleft{}to roll,\textquotedblright{} on a very old root meaning \textquotedblleft{}to turn.\textquotedblright{} English borrowed the Latin verb several times over and kept the rolling in every one: \textbf{revolve}, \textbf{involve}, \textbf{evolve}, a \textbf{volume} (a rolled scroll), a \textbf{vault} (a rolled arch).

Now listen to what happens when the stress lands on that \emph{o}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vuelvo}, \emph{vuelves}, \emph{vuelve} — the \emph{o} has broken into \emph{ue}.
\end{itemize}

That break reaches words carried down by mouth and leaves alone the ones lifted off a page. \emph{Volumen} and \emph{revolución} came out of books; their \emph{o} sits still. The same break already sits in \emph{puerta}, from Latin \emph{porta}.

The spelling has a wrinkle. Old Spanish wrote the verb \textbf{bolver}, with a \emph{b}, and that was the honest spelling for what people said. The modern \emph{v} is a later respelling aimed back at Latin \emph{volvere} — a change of ink, not of sound.

Three things to keep apart:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{revolver}, \textquotedblleft{}to stir,\textquotedblright{} really is \emph{re-} plus this verb, and it breaks the same way: \emph{revuelvo}.
  \item \textbf{revólver}, the firearm, is a separate word, borrowed from English in modern times. The stress has moved and an accent is written on it; that is the tell.
  \item \textbf{volver a} followed by another verb means doing that thing over — \emph{vuelvo a entrar}, \textquotedblleft{}I go in again.\textquotedblright{} No piece has been added to \emph{volver}. The pattern is an idiom, not a build.
\end{itemize}

And \emph{volar}, \textquotedblleft{}to fly,\textquotedblright{} is a stranger. Close in shape, unrelated in descent.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{volver}. And you can hear a broken \emph{o} as the sound of a word that never went through a book.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{volver}
  \item \emph{vuelvo}
  \item \emph{entrar y volver}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the \emph{o} do when the stress lands on it? (It breaks into \emph{ue} — \emph{vuelvo}.) And is \emph{revólver}, the firearm, this same word? (No — a modern borrowing from English, with its stress moved and an accent written on it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[llegar]{llegar — a ship brought to shore}

\label{lesson:ES-C395-llegar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to go in}, then \emph{to return}. (\emph{Entrar}; \emph{volver}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el barco — where the meaning began.
  \item lleno — the same \emph{ll-} out of the same \emph{pl-}.
  \item entrar — what you do after arriving.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ye-GAR}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{ll} is the \emph{y} of \emph{yes} across most of the Spanish-speaking world; the \emph{g} is hard, as in \emph{go}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{llegar} — \textquotedblleft{}to arrive.\textquotedblright{}

Take the secure half first: the \textbf{form}. Corominas gives the etymon as Latin \textbf{plicāre}, which he treats as a back-formation from the compound \emph{applicāre}.

The sound history holds it up. Latin words beginning \textbf{pl-} came into Spanish with \textbf{ll-} and into Portuguese with \textbf{ch-}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{lleno} / \emph{cheio};
  \item \textbf{lluvia} / \emph{chuva};
  \item \textbf{llorar} / \emph{chorar};
  \item \textbf{llegar} / \emph{chegar}.
\end{itemize}

Now the unsteady half: the \textbf{meaning}. Corominas does not bridge it with sails. His bridge is a sailors' phrase the most classical authors used constantly — \textbf{applicāre nāvem}, \textquotedblleft{}to bring a ship to shore,\textquotedblright{} \emph{frecuentísimo}, he calls it. The chain runs: to dock, then to arrive by sea, then to arrive anywhere.

He also declines to close the case, allowing in his own entry that there were \textbf{probably several semantic origins at once}. The form is settled; the story about the meaning is a probability, offered as one.

Two things to refuse.

The first is the tale you will meet everywhere: \emph{plicāre} meant \textquotedblleft{}to fold,\textquotedblright{} sailors folded their sails on arriving, so folding became arriving. No source argues it. It assumes arrival in order to explain arrival.

The second is a footnote that has escaped into the world. Both Wiktionaries give \emph{applicāre} as the etymon and hang Corominas's name on it. His entry gives \emph{plicāre} as the etymon and \emph{applicāre} only as the source of the sense. The name has travelled further than the claim it belongs to.

In fairness, the competing account is not empty: Spanish \textbf{allegar} and Portuguese \textbf{achegar} are exactly what \emph{applicāre} should have produced, and both exist. The paper trail is early too — \emph{aplekare} stands in the tenth-century Glosas Silenses, and \emph{llegar} is already in the Cid.

English takes the same root by the borrowed route: \textbf{apply}, \textbf{imply}, \textbf{employ}, \textbf{deploy}, \textbf{pliant}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{llegar}. And you have watched a citation outrun the claim it came from.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{llegar}
  \item \emph{llegar a la casa}
  \item \emph{llegar y entrar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{applicāre nāvem} mean? (To bring a ship to shore.) And what does a Spanish \emph{ll-} at the front of a word often answer to in Portuguese? (\emph{ch-} — \emph{lleno} beside \emph{cheio}, \emph{llegar} beside \emph{chegar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[perder]{perder — a second half nobody has settled}

\label{lesson:ES-C395-perder}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to return}, then \emph{to arrive}. (\emph{Volver}; \emph{llegar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la llave — the thing most often lost.
  \item buscar — what you do afterwards.
  \item perdón — the look-alike with a different build.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{per-DER}, two beats with the weight on the second. Both \emph{r}'s are one tap; the \emph{d} is soft, with the tongue against the teeth rather than behind them. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{perder} — \textquotedblleft{}to lose.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{perdere}, \textquotedblleft{}to destroy, to lose,\textquotedblright{} carried down by mouth. Its \emph{-dere} ending came out as \emph{-der} along the regular road, and you can hear the stressed vowel do the familiar thing: \emph{pierdo}, \emph{pierdes}, \emph{pierde} — the \emph{e} has broken into \emph{ie}, the same kind of break you heard in \emph{vuelvo}.

English holds the clean cognate in \textbf{perdition} — destruction, loss, total and final.

The front half of the Latin word is not in doubt: \textbf{per-}, \textquotedblleft{}through, thoroughly,\textquotedblright{} the piece that pushes a verb to its limit.

The back half is where careful sources part company, and this is the point of the lesson.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Etymonline reads it as \textbf{dare}, \textquotedblleft{}to give\textquotedblright{} — losing as giving something away completely.
  \item Wiktionary and de Vaan read it as a \textbf{separate element meaning \textquotedblleft{}to put\textquotedblright{}}, descended from a different old root, the one that also stands behind English \emph{do}.
\end{itemize}

The two ancient roots are close enough in shape that Wiktionary itself warns they are not always easy to tell apart. So the honest description of \emph{perdere} is: \textbf{per-} plus a verbal element whose identity is disputed. Anyone who hands you \textquotedblleft{}per- plus give\textquotedblright{} flat, with no hedge, has skipped a live argument.

One trap that catches learners. \emph{Perder} and \textbf{perdón} look like a matched pair and are not one. \emph{Perdón} rests on \emph{per-} plus \textbf{dōnāre}, and \emph{dōnāre} really does come from the \textquotedblleft{}give\textquotedblright{} root. Same prefix, different second half, and the second half is the whole question.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{perder}. And you have a case where good dictionaries split, and the accurate answer is to name the split.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{perder}
  \item \emph{pierdo la llave}
  \item \emph{llegar y perder}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the front half of \emph{perdere}, and how much of the back half is settled? (\emph{Per-}, \textquotedblleft{}thoroughly\textquotedblright{}; the back half is disputed — \textquotedblleft{}to give\textquotedblright{} or a separate element meaning \textquotedblleft{}to put.\textquotedblright{}) Is \emph{perdón} the same build? (No — \emph{per-} plus \emph{dōnāre}, which does rest on the \textquotedblleft{}give\textquotedblright{} root.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[necesitar]{necesitar — the word that came in through a book}

\label{lesson:ES-C395-necesitar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to arrive}, then \emph{to lose}. (\emph{Llegar}; \emph{perder}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item necesario — the adjective standing beside it.
  \item la ayuda — what you most often need.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ne-se-si-TAR}, four beats with the weight on the last. The \emph{c} before \emph{e} is a soft \emph{s} across the Americas and a \emph{th} across much of Spain. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{necesitar} — \textquotedblleft{}to need.\textquotedblright{}

This verb arrived by a different door from the others. Medieval Latin had \textbf{necessitō}; Spanish took it over from writing, and it is on record here by the seventeenth century — read in late off a page, not handed down mouth to mouth from the Romans. French \emph{nécessiter} is attested a good deal earlier, but no source claims the Spanish came through French, so that stays unsaid.

English draws on the same family: \textbf{necessary}, \textbf{necessity}, \textbf{necessitate}.

Now the interesting part, which is a lesson in reading dictionaries.

Inside Latin \textbf{necesse}, the two easiest sources answer without blinking. Both parse it as \emph{ne-} plus an element meaning \textquotedblleft{}yielded\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}backing away\textquotedblright{} — hence the tidy gloss, \textquotedblleft{}that from which there is no yielding.\textquotedblright{}

Baldi, writing in 2013, takes that apart. \emph{Necessus}, he says, \textbf{has resisted definitive analysis}. The \emph{nec} plus \emph{esse} account is a popular etymology with obvious shortcomings. And the particular \emph{cessus} form the tidy parse leans on does not turn up until the late Imperial period — far too late to be of any value.

Notice how the tidy gloss argues, too: it reads \textquotedblleft{}yielding\textquotedblright{} out of a reconstructed piece, then offers the word's own sense of the unavoidable back as proof. The conclusion sat in the premise.

So: the \textbf{ne-} is secure, and the rest is open. That is the whole of what can be said, and saying it beats borrowing someone else's confidence.

One construction note: this verb takes its object plain — \emph{necesito ayuda}, \textquotedblleft{}I need help.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Necesitar de} survives in archaic and literary writing.)
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five everyday actions: \emph{entrar}, \emph{volver}, \emph{llegar}, \emph{perder}, \emph{necesitar}. And a habit — when a source sounds surer than its evidence, keep the hedge.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Name all five actions, one after another, and add one thing you know about each.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{entrar} — and where you go in
  \item \emph{volver} — and what the \emph{o} does under stress
  \item \emph{llegar} — and what Portuguese puts at the front instead
  \item \emph{perder} — and what you lost
  \item \emph{necesitar} — and what you need
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Did \emph{necesitar} come down in speech or in from writing? (In from writing — Medieval Latin \emph{necessitō}, in Spanish by the seventeenth century.) Which piece of \emph{necesse} is secure? (The \emph{ne-}; the second element has resisted definitive analysis.)
\end{tcolorbox}
